    Integrating fast frequentist empirical-Bayes gene-expression dispersion estimation as a prior

    Stefano Mangiola

    Source: vignettes/dispersion-priors.Rmd
    dispersion-priors.Rmd

    brmDE, although very flexible and capable of mixed-effect models, non-parametric smooth/spline models, and alternative distributions such as NB and ZINB, fits one gene at a time to prioritise parallelisation. A single-gene likelihood cannot borrow strength across features, which is exactly what makes empirical-Bayes estimation of feature-wise negative-binomial dispersion useful when the number of replicates is small.

    Frequentist methods such as edgeR estimate gene-wise dispersion through empirical Bayes very efficiently, although generally within more constrained fixed-effect model structures.

    The key idea is to estimate gene dispersion cheaply with empirical Bayes, for example through edgeR or DESeq2, and use the resulting across-gene dispersion information as an approximate prior for brmDE. With enough information in the gene’s own counts, the posterior can still move away from the upstream empirical-Bayes estimate.

    The conceptual transition is from a likelihood over candidate dispersion values to a prior kernel for dispersion. For fixed observed data, the likelihood

    Lg(ϕ)=p(yg∣ϕ) L_g(\phi) = p(y_g\mid\phi)

    is a function of the candidate parameter value ϕ\phi. It is not itself a probability density for ϕ\phi. However, the empirical-Bayes machinery in edgeR constructs a weighted, abundance-smoothed log-likelihood contribution that represents information borrowed across genes. In brmDE, we use this weighted shared log-likelihood as an empirical prior kernel for the parameter that is actually modelled, log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi).

    This is an explicit modelling approximation: the edgeR weighted shared likelihood is not itself a Bayesian prior, but it can be used to define one.

    The maximum of this weighted smoothed likelihood defines the mode of the prior. Under the local Normal approximation developed below, the mode is also used as the prior mean. The prior width is obtained from the local curvature of the same weighted smoothed likelihood.

    Because the smoothed dispersion trend is returned directly by edgeR as trended.dispersion, the less intuitive part is the transition from the weighted shared likelihood to the prior SD. That calculation is described below.

    From smoothed shrunk likelihood to log-scale SD

    edgeR estimates an abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood and weights it through empirical Bayes. For gene gg, we denote this as

    wℓsmooth,g(ϕ), w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi),

    where

    w=𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚗. w=\texttt{prior.n}.

    In brmDE, the dispersion parameter is handled on the log scale. We therefore define the prior kernel directly as a function of log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi):

    log⁡pg(log(ϕ))∝wℓsmooth,g(elog⁡(ϕ)). \log p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) \propto w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}\left(e^{\log(\phi)}\right).

    This avoids introducing an unnecessary change-of-variable step from a density defined with respect to dϕd\phi to one defined with respect to dlog⁡(ϕ)d\log(\phi). We are explicitly defining the prior on the scale used by brmDE.

    The maximum of this prior kernel occurs at

    log⁡(ϕtrend,g), \log\left(\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}\right),

    where ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} is returned by edgeR as trended.dispersion.

    The weighted edgeR curve is not itself a Bayesian prior density. For constructing the brmDE prior, we use its local shape around the maximum.

    Intuitive route from weighted smoothed likelihood to prior SD:

    1. Treat the weighted smoothed curve as an unnormalised log-density on the log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi) scale.
    2. Exponentiate it to obtain an unnormalised probability density.
    3. Normalise it so that its total area is 1.
    4. Calculate the mean and SD of that probability distribution.
    5. Equivalently, one could sample from the normalised density and calculate the empirical SD.
    6. A faster local approximation is to estimate the SD from the curvature around the mode.

    Why curvature can be calculated directly from the weighted log-likelihood

    We are calculating the curvature of the log of the normalised probability density, as a proxy for the curvature of the probability density itself.

    Define the weighted smoothed log-likelihood on the log-dispersion scale as

    qg(log(ϕ))=wℓsmooth,g(elog⁡(ϕ)). q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}\left(e^{\log(\phi)}\right).

    The corresponding normalised prior density can be written as

    pg(log(ϕ))=exp⁡[qg(log(ϕ))]Z, p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = \frac{ \exp\left[ q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) \right] }{ Z },

    where ZZ is the normalising constant.

    Taking the logarithm gives

    log⁡pg(log(ϕ))=qg(log(ϕ))−log⁡Z. \log p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right)-\log Z.

    Since log⁡Z\log Z is constant with respect to log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi),

    d2d[log⁡(ϕ)]2log⁡pg(log(ϕ))=d2d[log⁡(ϕ)]2qg(log(ϕ)). \frac{d^2}{d[\log(\phi)]^2} \log p_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right) = \frac{d^2}{d[\log(\phi)]^2} q_g\!\left(\log(\phi)\right).

    Therefore,

    curvature of the log normalised prior=curvature of the weighted smoothed log-likelihood. \text{curvature of the log normalised prior} = \text{curvature of the weighted smoothed log-likelihood}.

    This means that the conceptual exponentiation and normalisation steps do not need to be carried out explicitly when estimating curvature.

    Numerical curvature from the edgeR likelihood grid

    The abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood is available numerically over a finite dispersion grid, so we estimate its local curvature from those grid values.

    Suppose there are GG genes and KK dispersion-grid points.

    • shared.loglik is a G×KG \times K matrix. Rows correspond to genes and columns correspond to dispersion-grid points.
    • shared.loglik[g, ] is therefore a numeric vector of length KK. It gives the y-values of the abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood for gene gg across candidate dispersions.
    • spline.pts is a numeric vector of length KK. It gives the grid coordinates corresponding to the KK columns of shared.loglik.
    • prior.n is the weight applied to the shared likelihood. In the standard non-robust case it is a scalar; with robust estimation it may be gene-specific.

    The x-axis used for the local fit is

    xk=log⁡(ϕk). x_k = \log(\phi_k).

    The corresponding y-axis is

    yk=wg×𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚛𝚎𝚍.𝚕𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚔[g,k], y_k = w_g \times \texttt{shared.loglik}[g,k],

    where wgw_g is prior.n for gene $gwhen gene-specific weights are used, or the common scalarprior.n` otherwise.

    Thus, for gene gg, the local fit uses the paired points

    (xk,yk)=(log(ϕk),wg×𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚛𝚎𝚍.𝚕𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚔[g,k]). \left( x_k, y_k \right) = \left( \log(\phi_k), \; w_g \times \texttt{shared.loglik}[g,k] \right).

    Local quadratic fit

    Rather than trying to derive probability distribution from smooth shrinked likelihood and sample from it to get the standard deviation, we use an approximate method.

    We estimate the curvature around the expected mode

    xtrend,g=log⁡(ϕtrend,g). x_{\mathrm{trend},g} = \log\left(\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}\right).

    We select a small number of grid points around the grid location closest to xtrend,gx_{\mathrm{trend},g} and define

    zk=xk−xtrend,g. z_k = x_k - x_{\mathrm{trend},g}.

    Since, smooth likelihood around their maximum tend to be quadratic in shape, we then fit the local quadratic model

    yk=a+bzk+czk2. y_k = a + b z_k + c z_k^2.

    This can be fitted directly with base R stats::lm() because the model is linear in the coefficients aa, bb, and cc.

    In R, the design formula is

    y[idx] ~ z + I(z^2)

    where

    z <- x[idx] - log(phi_trend_g)

    and idx identifies a small neighbourhood of grid points around the trended dispersion.

    The fitted design matrix has three columns:

    interceptzz211z1z1221z2z22⋮⋮⋮⋮n1znzn2 \begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{intercept} & z & z^2\\ \hline 1 & 1 & z_1 & z_1^2\\ 2 & 1 & z_2 & z_2^2\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\ n & 1 & z_n & z_n^2 \end{array}

    and lm() estimates

    a,b,c. a,\;b,\;c.

    The fitted function is therefore a parabola, not a straight line.

    The second derivative of the fitted quadratic is

    d2dz2(a+bz+cz2)=2c. \frac{d^2}{dz^2} \left( a+bz+cz^2 \right) = 2c.

    At a valid local maximum,

    c<0. c<0.

    We therefore define the positive local curvature as

    Ig=−2c. I_g = -2c.

    This estimates

    Ig=−d2d[log⁡(ϕ)]2[wℓsmooth,g(ϕ)]|ϕ=ϕtrend,g. I_g = - \left. \frac{d^2}{d[\log(\phi)]^2} \left[ w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) \right] \right|_{\phi=\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}}.

    A sharper peak gives larger positive curvature,

    sharp peak⇒Ig large, \text{sharp peak} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_g\text{ large},

    whereas a flatter peak gives smaller curvature,

    flat peak⇒Ig small. \text{flat peak} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_g\text{ small}.

    Convert curvature into a brms prior standard deviation

    The final step is a local Normal, or Laplace, approximation.

    Near its mode, a sufficiently smooth log-density can be approximated by a quadratic. For a Normal distribution,

    log⁡p(x)=C−(x−μ)22σ2, \log p(x) = C - \frac{ (x-\mu)^2 }{ 2\sigma^2 },

    so its curvature at the mode is

    1σ2. \frac{1}{\sigma^2}.

    Matching the Normal curvature to the local quadratic fit gives

    Ig=1σg2. I_g = \frac{1}{\sigma_g^2}.

    Since

    Ig=−2c, I_g=-2c,

    the prior variance is

    σg2=−12c. \sigma_g^2 = -\frac{1}{2c}.

    Therefore the local Normal approximation for the brmDE log-dispersion prior is

    log⁡(ϕg)≈N(log(ϕtrend,g),−12cg) \boxed{ \log(\phi_g) \approx N\left( \log(\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}), -\frac{1}{2c_g} \right) }

    with

    cg<0. c_g<0.

    The centre of the prior therefore comes from trended.dispersion, while its width is derived from the local curvature of the weighted shared edgeR likelihood.

    In brmDE the default width is the Laplace SD. estimate_dispersion_prior() writes two columns: dispersion_prior_log_mean (trended.dispersion) and dispersion_prior_log_sd (a width on log⁡ϕ\log\phi). method = "curvature" (default) fills that SD from the local quadratic of the weighted shared log-likelihood; method = "degrees_freedom" fills it from the trigamma SD of the moderated df. Pass both names to estimate_gene() / estimate(). The location is the offset on shape ~ 1 + offset(log(1/dispersion_prior_log_mean)). The intercept prior is Student-t, with scale chosen so that its standard deviation equals that log-scale σg\sigma_g.

    Appendix 1: edgeR calculation of the smoothed weighted likelihood

    disclamer: the following section should not be taken as substitute of the official edgeR literature (see references). It is just a convenient complement. For any divergence, the official literature should be considered instead.

    1. Each gene has a likelihood curve over candidate dispersions

    For gene gg, with observed counts ygy_g, edgeR evaluates the negative-binomial likelihood

    Lg(ϕ)=p(yg∣ϕ). L_g(\phi) = p(y_g\mid\phi).

    Usually we work with the log-likelihood

    ℓg(ϕ)=log⁡p(yg∣ϕ). \ell_g(\phi) = \log p(y_g\mid\phi).

    The data ygy_g are fixed, while ϕ\phi varies over a grid of candidate dispersion values,

    ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕK. \phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots,\phi_K.

    Across genes, this produces a matrix such as

    ϕ1ϕ2ϕ3ϕ4g1ℓ1(ϕ1)ℓ1(ϕ2)ℓ1(ϕ3)ℓ1(ϕ4)g2ℓ2(ϕ1)ℓ2(ϕ2)ℓ2(ϕ3)ℓ2(ϕ4)g3ℓ3(ϕ1)ℓ3(ϕ2)ℓ3(ϕ3)ℓ3(ϕ4) \begin{array}{c|cccc} & \phi_1 & \phi_2 & \phi_3 & \phi_4\\ \hline g_1 & \ell_1(\phi_1) & \ell_1(\phi_2) & \ell_1(\phi_3) & \ell_1(\phi_4)\\ g_2 & \ell_2(\phi_1) & \ell_2(\phi_2) & \ell_2(\phi_3) & \ell_2(\phi_4)\\ g_3 & \ell_3(\phi_1) & \ell_3(\phi_2) & \ell_3(\phi_3) & \ell_3(\phi_4) \end{array}

    Each row is one gene-specific log-likelihood curve over ϕ\phi.

    2. edgeR smooths each dispersion column over abundance

    Each gene has an abundance value AgA_g.

    For one fixed candidate dispersion ϕk\phi_k, edgeR has the log-likelihood values

    ℓ1(ϕk),ℓ2(ϕk),…,ℓG(ϕk). \ell_1(\phi_k), \ell_2(\phi_k), \ldots, \ell_G(\phi_k).

    It smooths these values against abundance:

    Ag→ℓg(ϕk). A_g \longrightarrow \ell_g(\phi_k).

    With the default edgeR implementation, this smoothing uses local regression through locfit.

    For every fixed candidate dispersion ϕk\phi_k, edgeR therefore obtains a smooth function of abundance, fk(A)f_k(A).

    For example,

    f1(A) f_1(A)

    describes the expected log-likelihood at dispersion ϕ1\phi_1 for a gene of abundance AA, while

    f2(A) f_2(A)

    does the same for ϕ2\phi_2, and so on.

    3. For one abundance, reconstruct the smoothed log-likelihood curve over dispersion

    Consider a particular gene gg with abundance AgA_g.

    For every candidate dispersion,

    ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕK, \phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots,\phi_K,

    edgeR evaluates the corresponding abundance-smoothed function at AgA_g:

    f1(Ag),f2(Ag),…,fK(Ag). f_1(A_g), f_2(A_g), \ldots, f_K(A_g).

    These values are placed side by side across dispersion:

    ϕϕ1ϕ2⋯ϕKsmoothed log-likelihoodℓsmooth,g(ϕ1)ℓsmooth,g(ϕ2)⋯ℓsmooth,g(ϕK) \begin{array}{c|cccc} \phi & \phi_1 & \phi_2 & \cdots & \phi_K\\ \hline \text{smoothed log-likelihood} & \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi_1) & \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi_2) & \cdots & \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi_K) \end{array}

    Together, these values define the function

    ℓsmooth,g(ϕ). \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi).

    This corresponds to edgeR’s internal notation m0g(ϕ)m_{0g}(\phi); for clarity, we use ℓsmooth,g(ϕ)\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) throughout.

    In the edgeR implementation:

    • trended.dispersion is returned by estimateDisp() and gives the abundance-dependent dispersion trend;
    • m0 is the internal matrix of local shared log-likelihoods;
    • prior.n is the weight applied to the shared likelihood contribution;
    • tagwise.dispersion is the final gene-specific moderated dispersion estimate.

    Thus,

    ℓsmooth,g(ϕ)↔𝚖𝟶, \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) \longleftrightarrow \texttt{m0},

    and

    w↔𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚗. w \longleftrightarrow \texttt{prior.n}.

    The abundance-dependent maximum of the shared likelihood corresponds to

    ϕtrend,g↔𝚝𝚛𝚎𝚗𝚍𝚎𝚍.𝚍𝚒𝚜𝚙𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗. \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} \longleftrightarrow \texttt{trended.dispersion}.

    m0 is an internal intermediate quantity and is not normally retained as a component of the DGEList returned by estimateDisp(). If brmDE needs the full shared likelihood curve, the relevant edgeR internal calculation must therefore be called, reproduced, or wrapped so that this matrix is retained.

    The whole curve

    ℓsmooth,g(ϕ) \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi)

    can be interpreted as:

    According to the likelihood behaviour of genes with similar abundance, how compatible is each candidate dispersion ϕ\phi?

    4. The maximum of this curve gives the trended dispersion

    edgeR finds the dispersion value at which the smoothed log-likelihood is maximal:

    ϕtrend,g=arg⁡maxϕℓsmooth,g(ϕ). \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} = \arg\max_{\phi} \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi).

    Thus ℓsmooth,g(ϕ)\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) is the whole curve, whereas ϕtrend,g\phi_{\mathrm{trend},g} is one value of ϕ\phi: the dispersion preferred by the across-gene information for a gene with abundance AgA_g.

    Repeating this operation over abundance produces the dispersion-abundance trend,

    A→ϕtrend(A). A \longrightarrow \phi_{\mathrm{trend}}(A).

    5. edgeR weights the across-gene log-likelihood curve

    edgeR estimates prior degrees of freedom through its empirical-Bayes procedure and converts these into the likelihood weight used by the weighted-likelihood machinery.

    In the standard non-robust implementation,

    𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚗=𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚍𝚏𝚗𝚕𝚒𝚋𝚜−𝚗𝚌𝚘𝚎𝚏𝚜. \texttt{prior.n} = \frac{ \texttt{prior.df} }{ \texttt{nlibs}-\texttt{ncoefs} }.

    With robust estimation, prior.df and therefore prior.n may be gene-specific.

    The weight controls how strongly the across-gene information contributes relative to the likelihood of the individual gene.

    A larger weight means stronger shrinkage towards the across-gene dispersion trend.

    The weighted curve is

    wℓsmooth,g(ϕ). w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi).

    Multiplying the log-likelihood by a positive weight does not change the location of its maximum:

    arg⁡maxϕwℓsmooth,g(ϕ)=ϕtrend,g. \arg\max_{\phi} w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) = \phi_{\mathrm{trend},g}.

    It does change the sharpness of the curve.

    A larger ww amplifies differences between candidate dispersion values and produces a sharper curve. A smaller ww produces a flatter curve.

    On the ordinary likelihood scale, multiplying the log-likelihood by ww is equivalent to raising the likelihood to the power ww:

    exp⁡[wℓsmooth,g(ϕ)]=[exp(ℓsmooth,g(ϕ))]w. \exp\left[ w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) \right] = \left[ \exp\left( \ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi) \right) \right]^w.

    For the edgeR tagwise dispersion, this weighted across-gene component is combined with the gene’s own log-likelihood.

    For brmDE, the gene’s own likelihood should not be included in the prior because the same gene will subsequently be fitted by brms. The relevant prior information is therefore the weighted across-gene curve

    wℓsmooth,g(ϕ). w\,\ell_{\mathrm{smooth},g}(\phi).

    Appendix 2: Where edgeR’s dispersion and the brms shape differ

    The design. estimateDisp() fits a fixed-effects GLM, so a random-effect term has to be handled somehow, and the two available choices bias ϕg\phi_g in opposite directions. Stripping it, for example passing ~ dex while brms fits ~ dex + (1 | cell), leaves the between-cell variance nowhere to go but ϕg\phi_g, inflating it. Passing the fixed-effect analogue (~ dex + cell) estimates those cell effects without shrinkage, so they absorb more variance than the mixed model’s partially pooled ones will, leaving ϕg\phi_g below the conditional shape brms is going to estimate. The target sits between the two:

    ϕedgeR(∼dex+cell)≤ϕbrmsconditional≤ϕedgeR(∼dex), \phi^{(\sim\,\mathrm{dex}\,+\,\mathrm{cell})}_{\mathrm{edgeR}} \;\le\; \phi^{\mathrm{conditional}}_{\mathrm{brms}} \;\le\; \phi^{(\sim\,\mathrm{dex})}_{\mathrm{edgeR}},

    with the position depending on how hard the mixed model shrinks, which is not known before fitting.

    The fixed-effect analogue also costs residual degrees of freedom. On airway’s 8 samples, ~ dex + cell spans 5 columns and leaves d=3d=3, whereas ~ dex leaves d=6d=6. This reduction in residual degrees of freedom increases the sampling uncertainty of the gene-wise residual dispersion estimates and can therefore affect the empirically estimated d0d_0. Because the brmDE prior width is ultimately calibrated from d0d_0, the choice of fixed-effect approximation can indirectly change the prior width.

    The family. The default is zero-inflated negative binomial. shape there is the same parameter as in negbinomial(), with the same NB kernel and the same log link; what differs is the estimand. It describes the count component, whereas edgeR fits a plain negative binomial to the marginal counts.

    Zero inflation contributes overdispersion quadratic in μ\mu exactly as the NB dispersion does, so a marginal fit sees the two combined. Matching Var(Y)=E[Y]+ϕE[Y]2\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathrm{E}[Y] + \phi\,\mathrm{E}[Y]^2 against the zero-inflated moments gives

    ϕmarginal=ϕ+π1−π,π=𝚣𝚒, \phi_{\mathrm{marginal}} = \frac{\phi+\pi}{1-\pi}, \qquad \pi=\texttt{zi},

    which pins both the direction and the size of that mismatch. edgeR’s estimate exceeds the ZINB component’s ϕ\phi whenever π>0\pi>0, by roughly π\pi in absolute terms and π/ϕ\pi/\phi in relative terms, so genes with small dispersion are the most distorted. The same expression is why zi and shape are only weakly separated: the mean-variance relationship constrains the combination, not the pair, leaving the shape of the zero mass as the main information that distinguishes them.

    The Student-t prior

    There are two important situations in which the edgeR dispersion trend can be systematically displaced from the dispersion estimated by brmDE (see Appendix 1).

    • Because edgeR dispersion estimation cannot fit mixed-effects models, a mixed-effects brmDE model must be approximated by a fixed-effects model. For example, ~ treatment + (1 | hospital) may be approximated by ~ treatment + hospital. The fixed effects are estimated without partial pooling and can absorb more variation, potentially reducing the residual negative-binomial dispersion.

    • A zero-inflated negative-binomial model in brmDE must be approximated upstream by an ordinary negative-binomial model. Zero inflation can then be absorbed by the edgeR negative-binomial dispersion, potentially increasing the estimated dispersion.

    For these cases, call estimate_dispersion_prior(..., method = "degrees_freedom"): the same Student-t intercept prior, but with dispersion_prior_log_sd filled from the log-scale SD ψ′(deff/2)\sqrt{\psi'(d_{\mathrm{eff}}/2)} implied by the moderated effective df deff=dresidual+d0d_{\mathrm{eff}} = d_{\mathrm{residual}} + d_0 (prior.df from squeezeVar() / estimateDisp()). tidybulk writes the df as dispersion_degrees_freedom; convert it with the same trigamma formula, or let estimate_dispersion_prior() do it. The default method = "curvature" is the local Laplace approximation of the weighted smoothed shared log-likelihood derived above.

    Appendix 3: Examples of how to use R formulas approximate a mixed-effect model with a fixed-effect one

    edgeR and DESeq2 have no random effects. To obtain the most relevant dispersion estimate, we can approximate the model fitted in brmDE using its fixed-effect analogue: drop the | and promote the grouping factor to a fixed term. If the random term also has a slope, include the interaction.

    Mixed-effect model (brmDE) Fixed-effect analogue (estimate_dispersion())
    ~ treatment + (1 \| hospital) ~ treatment + hospital
    ~ treatment + (1 \| hospital) + (1 \| batch) ~ treatment + hospital + batch
    ~ treatment + (treatment \| hospital) ~ treatment * hospital

    The last row is the random-slope case: (treatment | hospital) is (1 + treatment | hospital), so the analogue needs hospital-specific intercepts and hospital-specific treatment effects, which is treatment * hospital.

    Do not expand a nested random intercept (1 | hospital/ward) as hospital / ward. That formula is hospital + hospital:ward, which is rank-deficient when every ward belongs to one hospital, and edgeR will not fit it. Use the innermost grouping instead, uniquely coded: ~ treatment + ward.

    Illustration: the local quadratic approximation on airway

    The default prior width (estimate_dispersion_prior(..., method = "curvature")) treats edgeR’s weighted, abundance-smoothed shared log-likelihood as an unnormalised log-density on log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi), and replaces it with a Normal whose SD matches the local curvature at the mode. That is a local quadratic, not a claim that the whole curve is Gaussian.

    The following uses the airway dexamethasone experiment to look at that approximation. After dropping low-count genes, the shared log-likelihood is rebuilt on the same Cox–Reid grid and WLEB() smooth that estimateDisp() uses. plotBCV() shows the abundance–dispersion trend those curves sit on. Then 25 genes spanning the abundance range are drawn as

    xk=log⁡(ϕk),yk=𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛.𝚗g×𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚛𝚎𝚍.𝚕𝚘𝚐𝚕𝚒𝚔[g,k], x_k = \log(\phi_k), \qquad y_k = \texttt{prior.n}_g \times \texttt{shared.loglik}[g, k],

    the same plot(x, y) estimate_dispersion_prior() builds internally. The dashed vertical line is log⁡(𝚝𝚛𝚎𝚗𝚍𝚎𝚍.𝚍𝚒𝚜𝚙𝚎𝚛𝚜𝚒𝚘𝚗)\log(\texttt{trended.dispersion}), the mode at which the quadratic is fitted. The orange curve is the Laplace Normal on that same log-density scale: N(log⁡ϕtrend,σ2)N(\log\phi_{\mathrm{trend}}, \sigma^2) with σ\sigma from the local curvature, shifted to agree with yy at the mode.

    library(brmDE)
library(tidybulk)
library(tidySummarizedExperiment)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

data("airway", package = "airway")

airway <- airway |>
  mutate(
    dex = relevel(factor(dex), ref = "untrt"),
    cell = droplevels(cell)
  )

se <- airway |>
  keep_abundant(formula_design = ~ dex)

nrow(se)
#> [1] 15926

    keep_abundant() drops the low-count genes (identify_abundant() would only flag them). The design is the fixed-effect analogue of ~ dex + (1 | cell).

    design <- model.matrix(
  ~ dex + cell,
  data = as.data.frame(colData(se))
)
shared <- brmDE:::edger_shared_loglik(
  assay(se, "counts"),
  design
)

# x <- log(0.1 * 2^spline.pts). estimateDisp() uses 21 points on
# spline.pts in [-10, 10]; we use 61 on [-20, 10] so the curve is not
# stuck on two coarse ticks.
x <- log(shared$phi)

    edgeR’s plotBCV() is the abundance–dispersion trend on the same filtered matrix and design. BCV is ϕ\sqrt{\phi}. Each point is a gene’s tagwise estimate; the line is trended.dispersion, the mode of the shared curve in the facets below. On airway that trend is real but narrow, which is why those peaks sit near the same log⁡(ϕ)\log(\phi).

    dge <- edgeR::DGEList(SummarizedExperiment::assay(se, "counts"))
dge <- edgeR::calcNormFactors(dge)
dge <- edgeR::estimateDisp(dge, design)
edgeR::plotBCV(dge)

    Twenty-five genes spanning abundance: order the filtered genes by edgeR AveLogCPM, split that list into 25 equal slices, and take the middle gene of each slice, except the last slice, which uses the most abundant gene so the range is not truncated. Facets run from lowest to highest abundance. The strip shows CPM (2^AveLogCPM), not the log2 value. The black line is y = prior.n * shared.loglik[g, ]; the orange line is the Normal approximation from that gene’s local curvature.

    ave_log_cpm <- edgeR::aveLogCPM(assay(se, "counts"))
cpm <- 2^ave_log_cpm
ord <- order(ave_log_cpm)
n <- length(ord)
breaks <- floor(seq(1, n + 1, length.out = 26))
idx <- vapply(seq_len(25), function(i) {
  sl <- ord[seq.int(breaks[[i]], breaks[[i + 1L]] - 1L)]
  if (i == 25L) {
    sl[[length(sl)]]
  } else {
    sl[[ceiling(length(sl) / 2)]]
  }
}, integer(1))

genes <- rownames(se)[idx]
Y <- shared$prior.n[idx] * shared$shared.loglik[idx, , drop = FALSE]
x_mode <- log(shared$trended.dispersion[idx])
sigma <- vapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
  brmDE:::dispersion_quadratic_log_sd(x, Y[i, ], x_mode[[i]])
}, numeric(1))
panel <- sprintf(
  "%s\nCPM = %s\nσ = %.2f",
  genes,
  format(round(cpm[idx], 2), trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE),
  sigma
)

plot_df <- tibble(
  gene = factor(
    rep(panel, each = length(x)),
    levels = panel
  ),
  log_phi = rep(x, times = length(idx)),
  y = as.vector(t(Y))
)

x_fine <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 201)
approx_df <- lapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
  y <- Y[i, ]
  mu <- x_mode[[i]]
  s <- sigma[[i]]
  y0 <- y[[which.min(abs(x - mu))]]
  y_n <- y0 - (x_fine - mu)^2 / (2 * s^2)
  keep <- is.finite(y_n) & y_n >= min(y, na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(
    gene = factor(panel[[i]], levels = panel),
    log_phi = x_fine[keep],
    y = y_n[keep]
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

trend_df <- tibble(
  gene = factor(panel, levels = panel),
  log_phi_trend = x_mode
)
    
ggplot(plot_df, aes(log_phi, y)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = "edgeR weighted shared log-likelihood")) +
  geom_line(
    data = approx_df,
    aes(colour = "Laplace Normal"),
    linetype = 22
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = trend_df,
    aes(xintercept = log_phi_trend),
    linetype = 2,
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "edgeR weighted shared log-likelihood" = "black",
      "Laplace Normal" = "#d95f02"
    )
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y", ncol = 5) +
  labs(
    x = expression(log(phi)),
    y = "prior.n × shared.loglik",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 7),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 6),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
